disease.disease_type.sql_expression: CASE WHEN instr(disease_type, ' || ') > 0 THEN substr(disease_type, 1, instr(disease_type, ' || ') - 1) ELSE disease_type END
disease.disease_type.mapping_rule: Take the first item of the ' || '-separated list; values without the separator are unchanged.
disease.disease_type.reason: The query groups by disease_type as if each disease has one category label. Storing multi-type lists as combined strings (e.g. 'infectious || inflammatory') splits counts into many one-off combination groups. A single-column expression cannot duplicate a row under each of its types, so the first-listed type is the closest single-label form. The first item is taken as the primary classification, which assumes the document lists it first. Keeping the raw values would not match the author's per-category counts.

The LIKE underscore wildcard matches any single character, but no stored value contains a near-miss such as 'high mortality' or 'highXmortality' that would cause a false positive. The stored format already fits the query as written.

disease.disease_name.sql_expression: TRIM(CASE WHEN INSTR(disease_name, ' || ') > 0 THEN SUBSTR(disease_name, 1, INSTR(disease_name, ' || ') - 1) ELSE disease_name END)
disease.disease_name.reason: Many stored values are lists joined by ' || ', so an exact-match join to drug.disease_name and a GROUP BY on the full string fail for those diseases. Taking the first list item gives the disease's primary name, which matches the single-name entries used elsewhere (e.g., 'Asthma', 'Depression', 'COVID-19').

drug.disease_name.sql_expression: TRIM(CASE WHEN instr(disease_name, ' || ') > 0 THEN substr(disease_name, 1, instr(disease_name, ' || ') - 1) ELSE disease_name END)
drug.disease_name.reason: The query joins drug.disease_name to disease.disease_name on equality, so each drug must carry one disease name. The column is defined as the main disease the drug treats, and list values are stored as 'A || B' with the main disease first. Taking the text before the first ' || ' (or the whole value when there is no separator) yields that main disease for every row, and TRIM removes stray spaces. The remaining differences in spelling and case against the partner table are a separate issue and are not addressed by this expression.

drug.single_dose.mapping_rule: Map each distinct stored value to one numeric mg figure: the first listed dose, taken from the first population or item in any ' || ' list, with its number read in mg (e.g., '1 mg || 2 mg' becomes 1; '2.5mg || 5mg || 10mg || 20mg' becomes 2.5; 'adults 325 mg' becomes 325; 'adults 3.6mg/kg' becomes 3.6, since a per-kg figure is kept as its number). Values that are not stated ('not stated', 'not stated in document', 'Not stated in document', 'small dosages', "as per doctor's prescription", 'One pill', 'a few drops...', and similar non-quantified text) become NULL so the WHERE clause excludes them. Where the first item is a count of tablets or capsules with no mg amount, map to NULL unless a mg amount is given.
drug.single_dose.reason: The query compares single_dose numerically as CAST(... AS REAL). Most stored values are free text, lists, or units other than mg, and SQLite cannot reliably pull the first number out of them with a short deterministic expression. CAST alone would read text starting with words as 0, which would wrongly put 'not stated' and similar rows in the 'under 10 mg' bucket. A per-value mapping to the first listed mg dose, with NULL for unquantified values, gives the query the single numeric dose it expects.
